angles.title: Angles in radians, and why small angles are easy
angles.mini: An angle in radians is the arc it cuts divided by the radius: a full turn is 2π. For a thin triangle, the small side over the long side is almost the angle itself: {{sa1}} % off at 1°.
angles.text: An angle θ in radians is the arc s it cuts on a circle divided by the radius r: a full turn is 2πr / r = 2π rad, so 1 rad = 57.30°. A degree splits into 60 minutes of arc and a minute into 60 seconds of arc; 1″ is {{arcsecRad}} millionths of a radian. Every formula of physics computes in radians. For a long thin right triangle, the short side h over the long side d is almost the angle itself: tan θ ≈ sin θ ≈ θ, off by {{sa1}} % at 1°, {{sa5}} % at 5° and {{sa10}} % at 10°. That is why an object of height h at a distance d spans an angle of about h/d, and why the dip of the horizon can be written √(2h/R). Since 2019 the units themselves are fixed by constants of nature [1].
angles.labels: The radian: an arc measured in radii|Small angles: θ ≈ h / d
vectors.title: Adding vectors: Chasles' relation, components, subtraction
vectors.mini: From A to B then B to C lands where A to C does: AB⃗ + BC⃗ = AC⃗. Only the start and the end count. With components it is ordinary addition, axis by axis; subtracting is adding the arrow turned round.
vectors.text: Going from A to B, then from B to C, ends at the same place as going straight from A to C: with displacement vectors, AB⃗ + BC⃗ = AC⃗. This is Chasles' relation, after the French geometer Michel Chasles, and it holds for any number of steps: AB⃗ + BC⃗ + CD⃗ = AD⃗. Only the start and the end count, not the path; a round trip adds up to the zero vector, so BA⃗ = −AB⃗. It works the same for velocities, accelerations and forces. With components it is ordinary addition: put the arrows end to end and their shadows on each axis add up too, so a⃗ + b⃗ = (aₓ + bₓ, a_y + b_y). Subtracting is adding the opposite: a⃗ − b⃗ = a⃗ + (−b⃗), and drawn from a common origin it is the arrow from the tip of b⃗ to the tip of a⃗, the step still needed to get from one to the other. That is how a change of velocity Δv⃗ = v⃗₂ − v⃗₁ is drawn, and how a velocity seen from a moving train, v⃗′ = v⃗ − V⃗, is found.
vectors.labels: Chasles: AB⃗ + BC⃗ = AC⃗|Components add axis by axis|Subtraction: a⃗ − b⃗ = a⃗ + (−b⃗)
deriv.title: dx/dt, ẋ, x′: one derivative, three ways to write it
deriv.mini: Shrink the time interval to zero and the chord becomes the tangent: its slope is the derivative. Leibniz wrote dx/dt, Newton ẋ, Lagrange x′; the integral ∫ undoes it, and ∇ collects the slopes in every direction.
deriv.text: A derivative is a rate of change at one instant. Shrink the interval Δt of the mean velocity towards zero and the chord turns into the tangent to the curve; its slope is the instantaneous velocity. Newton and Leibniz found this independently and wrote it differently, and Lagrange added a third notation [1]: dx/dt (Leibniz) keeps the memory of a ratio of two tiny changes, ẋ with a dot (Newton) is used for derivatives with respect to time, x′ (Lagrange) says “derivative of x” without naming the variable. Two dots, two primes or d²x/dt² is the derivative taken twice, the acceleration. The integral ∫ undoes the derivative: adding the thin slices v dt gives the distance covered, the area under the curve of velocity. When a quantity depends on several variables, such as the height of a hill on a map, ∂h/∂x is its slope walking east with the other variable held fixed, and the gradient ∇h collects these partial derivatives into an arrow pointing straight uphill, across the contour lines.
deriv.labels: The tangent: dx/dt|The integral: ∫ v dt|The gradient: ∇h
sigma.title: A measurement is a value with its uncertainty
sigma.mini: Twelve stopwatch timings of a pendulum scatter by σ = {{stSd}} s around their mean, {{stMean}} s; the mean itself is known to σ/√12 = {{stSem}} s. Scatter is precision; closeness to the true value is accuracy.
sigma.text: Time the period of a 1 m pendulum twelve times by hand and you never get the same number twice: reaction time adds a random error each time. The mean is the best estimate; the standard deviation σ says how far one timing typically falls from it, and the mean is better known than any single timing, to σ/√N [1]. For the twelve timings in the histogram, invented for the example, x̄ = {{stMean}} s, σ = {{stSd}} s and σ/√N = {{stSem}} s; with the pendulum law T = 2π√(L/g) [2] that gives g = {{gSt}} ± {{gStErr}} m/s². About two thirds of the measurements fall within ±1σ, 95 % within ±2σ, and a value 3σ away has a 0.3 % chance of being bad luck. Random errors shrink when averaged; a systematic error, a watch running fast, shifts every measurement the same way and averaging does nothing against it. The targets show the difference between precision (tight grouping) and accuracy (centred on the true value).
sigma.labels: Twelve timings: mean and ±σ|Precision and accuracy
lsq.title: Least squares: the line that fits best
lsq.mini: To fit a model to measured points, choose its parameters so that the sum of the squared gaps is smallest. Five pendulum lengths, T² against L: the slope {{fitB}} s²/m gives g = {{gFit}} ± {{gFitErr}} m/s².
lsq.text: Least squares, published by Legendre in 1805 and Gauss in 1809 [1]: to fit a model f to measured points, choose its parameters so that χ², the sum of the squared gaps between the points and the model (the residuals), each divided by its uncertainty, is as small as possible. Here, five pendulum lengths L and the square of their periods T², numbers invented for the example: the pendulum law says T² = (4π²/g) L, a straight line through zero. The best line has a slope of {{fitB}} ± {{fitSb}} s²/m, so g = {{gFit}} ± {{gFitErr}} m/s². The residuals, enlarged twelve times in orange, scatter on both sides of the line with no pattern, as they should when the model is right. When the residuals of a model are much larger than the measurement uncertainty, or follow a pattern, that model does not describe the data.
demmesh.title: A terrain model is a mesh: why a summit comes out lower
demmesh.mini: An invented summit, gridded every 5, 10, 20 and 40 m: the nodes that go come down onto the coarser surface, and the summit read on the mesh drops below the real one. Then a hole, filled by another model that does not meet the first.
demmesh.text: A terrain model stores one height per node, and the site reads between the four nodes of a cell by a weighted mean (bilinear interpolation). The weights add up to 1, so the mesh never rises above its highest node: a sharp summit that falls between nodes is lost. On an invented summit at true scale, the grid goes from 5 to 40 m and the summit read on the mesh drops; 1 m LiDAR [1] loses centimetres, a 30 m model [2] can lose tens of metres. Where the LiDAR has a hole, another model fills it: made another way, it does not meet the first at the edges, and gives yet another summit. The heights are invented for the example.
